## Problem

`sweep (macos, full suite)` fails on `main`, and that job is not `continue-on-error`, so it is
what turns the mirror Test Suite red. It began at `5aa0eef98fd` (2026-09-20T18:45Z); the prior
run `35511654149` at `e84e4c5e943` was green. Confirmed in run `35551741150`, job
`106187634021`.

Four tests fail, all in `tests/infra/test_mcp_entrypoint.py`:

- `test_clean_code_workspace_behind_origin_main_fast_forwards`
- `test_refresh_emits_workspace_sha_and_distance_from_target`
- `test_missing_workspace_is_recloned`
- `test_workspace_with_unresolvable_head_is_recloned`

The first two assert on output containing:

```
/Users/runner/work/rebar/rebar/infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh: line 74: flock: command not found
mcp: timed out waiting for the tickets ensure lock
mcp: tickets store ensure deferred (see logs)
```

The last two then fail downstream with
`CalledProcessError: ['git','-C',...,'rev-parse','HEAD'] returned non-zero exit status 128`,
because the store was never provisioned.

## Root cause

`infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh` defines `with_dir_lock()`, which serializes every
shared-volume write. It opens fd 9 on the directory inode and calls:

```sh
if ! flock -w "$MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT" 9; then
```

`flock(1)` ships with util-linux. macOS has no such binary, so the call fails with
`command not found` (exit 127). The `if !` branch fires, `with_dir_lock` returns 1, and the
caller defers the tickets-store ensure. Every later step that assumes a provisioned store then
fails, which is the `rev-parse HEAD` exit 128.

This is a hard dependency on a Linux-only binary in a script that also runs on macOS.

## Second, distinct defect in the same branch

The failure is reported as `mcp: timed out waiting for the ... lock`. That message is wrong: a
missing binary is not a timeout. `flock` exit 127 (not found) and exit 1 (genuinely could not
acquire within `-w`) are collapsed into one message, so the real cause is masked. The CI log
only reveals it because the shell separately prints `flock: command not found`. Any operator
reading only rebar's own output is told the wrong thing.

## Design constraints

The replacement must:

1. Work on macOS and Linux with no new installed dependency. `flock(1)` is not installable as a
   baseline assumption on macOS runners or developer machines.
2. Preserve the existing serialization contract described in the comment above `with_dir_lock`:
   overlapping asynchronous provisioning, `restart:always`, and operator restarts may contend
   outside the deploy mutex, so mutual exclusion must be real, not advisory-in-name.
3. Preserve the bounded wait: `MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT` seconds, then give up and return 1.
4. Preserve the current call shape: sequential, non-nested calls; fd 9 always closed; the
   wrapped command's exit status returned unchanged as `wdl_rc`.
5. Release the lock if the holder dies, so a crashed container cannot wedge provisioning
   permanently.

Constraint 5 is why a naive `mkdir`-based lock is not automatically correct: it leaves a stale
directory behind on crash unless staleness is handled explicitly. Whatever is chosen, crash
release must be demonstrated, not assumed.

`fcntl.flock` exists on both Linux and macOS and is reachable from the `python3` this image
already requires. If fd 9 is inherited by a child process, the lock lives on the open file
description shared by parent and child, so the child exiting does not release it while the
parent still holds fd 9. That is a candidate, not a conclusion: verify the release semantics
experimentally on macOS before relying on them.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1 The root cause is confirmed by reproducing `flock: command not found` from
  `with_dir_lock` on macOS; oracle: a recorded transcript.
- [x] AC2 `with_dir_lock` acquires and releases a real exclusive lock on macOS with no
  `flock(1)` present; oracle: a test that fails before the change and passes after.
- [x] AC3 Mutual exclusion is proven, not assumed: two concurrent holders cannot both enter the
  critical section; oracle: a concurrency test asserting serialized entry.
- [x] AC4 The bounded wait still honours `MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT` and returns 1 on genuine
  contention timeout; oracle: a test holding the lock past the wait.
- [x] AC5 A lock held by a process that dies is released, so provisioning is not wedged;
  oracle: a test that kills a holder and shows the next acquirer succeeds.
- [x] AC6 The wrapped command's exit status is still returned unchanged and fd 9 is closed on
  every path, including the failure path; oracle: tests asserting propagated status.
- [x] AC7 A missing-tool or unexpected-failure condition is no longer reported as a timeout;
  the message distinguishes "could not acquire within N seconds" from "lock mechanism
  unavailable"; oracle: tests asserting each message.
- [x] AC8 All four named tests in `tests/infra/test_mcp_entrypoint.py` pass on macOS; oracle:
  targeted pytest transcript, red before and green after.
- [x] AC9 Linux behaviour is unchanged; oracle: the same tests pass under CI's Linux cell.
- [x] AC10 The change adds no new installed dependency and no CI-provider-specific path;
  oracle: inspection of the script and its invocation.
- [x] AC11 `make verify` is clean apart from the 17 known macOS-arm64 pandoc `Bad CPU type`
  failures; oracle: the verify log's distinct-failure list.
- [x] AC12 `sweep (macos, full suite)` returns to green on `main` after this lands; oracle: the
  next mirror Test Suite run. [non-codebase]

## Blast radius

`infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh` is the MCP container entrypoint and guards the shared tickets
volume. A regression here can corrupt or wedge the shared store, so every change must keep the
serialization contract above. `tests/infra/test_mcp_entrypoint.py` is the existing oracle.

## Portability

The remedy is a shell/Python change inside the entrypoint, triggered by running the entrypoint
itself. It is not tied to GitHub Actions or any CI provider, and works with no CI at all.
